name: The Titanomachy: Cronus, the stone, and the ten-year war
scope: The generation-war that puts Zeus on the throne, told verbatim in Hesiod's Theogony. T1: CRONUS is the youngest of the twelve TITANS, children of GAIA (Earth) and OURANOS (Sky); he castrates his own father with a jagged SICKLE of adamant given to him by Gaia, and the drops of blood that fall on the earth produce the Furies (Theogony 154-187). Warned that he in turn will be overthrown by one of his own children, he SWALLOWS each newborn as his wife RHEA hands it over -- Hestia, Demeter, Hera, Hades and Poseidon go down one after another. T2: when the sixth child is due, Rhea hides herself away on the island of CRETE and gives birth in a cave on MOUNT IDA (some versions Mount Dikte); she then wraps a STONE in swaddling-clothes and hands the stone to Cronus, who swallows it thinking it is the baby (Theogony 485). The baby is ZEUS. T3: raised in secret in the Cretan cave, fed on the milk of the she-goat AMALTHEA (whose horn later becomes the cornucopia, the horn of plenty) and hidden by the noise of the KOURETES, young warrior-spirits who dance and clash their bronze shields to drown out the baby's crying so Cronus will not hear him. T4: grown up, Zeus makes Cronus VOMIT UP his swallowed siblings (in some versions with a herb given him by Metis) -- and the STONE comes up first, and Zeus sets it up at DELPHI as a memorial where later ages call it the OMPHALOS, the navel-stone of the world (Theogony 497-500, Pausanias 10.24.6). T5: the freed gods then fight a TEN-YEAR WAR against the Titans from Mount OLYMPUS; the tide turns when Zeus goes down into TARTARUS and frees the three ONE-EYED CYCLOPES (Brontes, Steropes, Arges) and the three HUNDRED-HANDED HECATONCHIRES (Cottus, Briareus, Gyges), imprisoned there by Ouranos. The Cyclopes forge for Zeus the THUNDERBOLT, for Poseidon the TRIDENT, and for Hades the CAP OF INVISIBILITY; the Hecatoncheires hurl three hundred boulders in a single volley (Theogony 713-720), the Titans are defeated and sealed in Tartarus behind bronze gates guarded by the Hundred-Handed, and Zeus, Poseidon and Hades draw lots for sky, sea, and underworld. Further rungs: the golden age under Cronus said to be the FIRST of Hesiod's five ages of man (Works and Days 109-126); the omphalos stone at Delphi was still shown to travellers in Pausanias's day in the 2nd c. CE; the Kouretes' clashing shields are the origin story for the Cretan armed dance still performed at festivals of Zeus.
source: PRIMARY: Hesiod, Theogony 154-187 (Cronus and the sickle), 453-506 (the swallowing, the stone, Rhea's escape to Crete, the vomiting-up), 617-720 (freeing the Cyclopes and Hundred-Handed, the forging of the thunderbolt, the ten-year war, the three-hundred-boulder volley). Also Apollodorus, Bibliotheca 1.1-1.2 (parallel prose account naming the Cretan cave and Amalthea); Pausanias, Description of Greece 10.24.6 (the omphalos stone shown at Delphi). CONSULTED: Grokipedia 'Titanomachy' and 'Cronus' (403; via browser 2026-09-04) and Wikipedia 'Titanomachy', 'Cronus', 'Rhea (mythology)' -- the swallowing of the children, the stone wrapped in swaddling-clothes, Mount Ida (Dikte in some versions), the goat Amalthea, the Kouretes clashing shields, freeing the Cyclopes to forge the thunderbolt/trident/cap, Hecatoncheires hurling boulders, Tartarus sealed. CORROBORATE AT BUILD: verify Hesiod line numbers for the stone-swallowing and the three-hundred-boulder passage before locking any quote-recall rung.
framing_note: The FOUNDATIONAL ladder of the whole Greek pillar -- every Olympian story assumes this backstory. Dinner-test payoff: T2 (Rhea handed him a STONE wrapped in a blanket and Cronus swallowed it) and T4 (that same stone was vomited back up FIRST and set up at Delphi as the navel-stone of the world -- and Pausanias reports travellers were still shown it centuries later). ANTI-RESTATEMENT: never let the stem name 'the stone' as the answer AND describe Rhea handing it over in the same rung; describe the SCENE (a Titan king swallowing his newborns, a mother hiding on Crete, a swaddled bundle) and let the recall be what was actually in the swaddling, the island, the goat's name, the omphalos. SYMMETRIC-VOICE: told with the same weight as the Norse Aesir-Vanir war or the Christian generation-war of angels -- a cosmic uprising against the old order. No 'primitive Greek belief', no scare-quoted gods. DISTRACTOR MINE: other generation-swallowing scenes (Ouranos hiding his children in Gaia's womb -- adjacent-real from the same Theogony), other Cretan-cave stories (Zeus's later love-affairs on Crete), other 'stone at the centre of the world' claims (Jerusalem Foundation Stone -- Jewish-Christian pillar, must not confuse). Wrong swords: not 'a scythe' (that is Cronus later iconography), not 'a spear' -- the sickle is HARPE.
history_overlap: GEOGRAPHY owns Mount Ida and the Cretan caves as places, Delphi as a sanctuary site, Olympus as a mountain; theology owns the STORY (baby hidden in the cave, stone set up at Delphi, gods on Olympus). HISTORY owns Bronze-Age Crete as archaeology; here Crete is the birthplace of a god.

name: Zeus: the thunderbolt, the eagle, the disguises
scope: The king of the gods and his working kit. T1: ZEUS is king of Olympus and lord of the sky; his weapon is the THUNDERBOLT (Greek 'keraunos'), forged for him in the Titanomachy by the three CYCLOPES (Brontes 'Thunder', Steropes 'Lightning', Arges 'Bright') in return for freeing them from Tartarus. His sacred bird is the EAGLE, said to have brought him the thunderbolt in its claws before every battle. T2: his other named gear -- the AEGIS, a goat-skin (from Amalthea, the she-goat who had suckled him on Crete) fringed with serpents and set with the head of the Gorgon Medusa in its centre, shaken to make thunder and terrify enemies (Iliad 5.738); and Athena often carries it on his behalf. T3: Zeus is famous for his DISGUISES to seduce mortal women -- he comes to LEDA (queen of Sparta) as a SWAN, and she lays TWO EGGS from which hatch Helen of Troy and the twins Castor and Pollux; to EUROPA (a Phoenician princess) as a WHITE BULL who kneels among her flowers on the beach at Tyre and carries her over the sea to Crete, where she bears him Minos (Ovid, Metamorphoses 2.836-875); to DANAE (locked by her father in a bronze tower) as a SHOWER OF GOLD falling through the roof, and she bears him Perseus. T4: he seduces ALKMENE (in Thebes) by taking the shape of her own husband Amphitryon returned from war and making the night three times as long -- the son born of that night is HERACLES. He seduces GANYMEDE (a beautiful Trojan prince) by sending the eagle down to snatch him up to Olympus to be cupbearer to the gods. T5: at PROMETHEUS's trick at Mecone Zeus chooses the sacrifice-portion covered in fat -- and finds bones under it -- and in fury denies mortals fire; when Prometheus steals fire back in a hollow FENNEL-STALK, Zeus chains him to a crag in the CAUCASUS and sends an EAGLE (his own bird) to eat his liver every day, the liver growing back every night, until Heracles shoots the eagle centuries later (Theogony 521-616). Further rungs: Zeus's siblings by lot -- Poseidon takes the sea, Hades the underworld, Zeus the sky (all three share the earth and Olympus); his wife HERA is also his SISTER; his oracle is at DODONA where his answers come from the rustling of a great OAK TREE; his most famous temple stands at OLYMPIA in the Peloponnese, home of the Games and site of the gold-and-ivory colossal seated Zeus of Pheidias, one of the Seven Wonders of the ancient world.
source: PRIMARY: Homer, Iliad 5.738-742 (the aegis with the Gorgon-head), 15.187-193 (the three brothers dividing sky/sea/underworld by lot); Hesiod, Theogony 139-146 (the three Cyclopes as thunderbolt-forgers), 521-616 (Prometheus's trick, fire in the fennel-stalk, the eagle at the liver); Ovid, Metamorphoses 2.836-875 (Zeus as the white bull carrying Europa), 4.610-644 (Danae and the shower of gold), 6.103-114 (the swan and Leda); Apollodorus, Bibliotheca 2.4.1 (Danae). framing_note: The BROAD-STROKE Zeus ladder -- the disguises are the dinner-test hooks (a swan? a bull? gold?). Dinner-test payoff: T3 (he came to LEDA as a SWAN and she laid two eggs; he carried EUROPA off as a white BULL from a Phoenician beach) and T5 (his own EAGLE is the one that eats Prometheus's liver every day). ANTI-RESTATEMENT: never let the stem say 'Zeus in the form of a swan' and then ask who came to Leda; describe the SCENE (a Spartan queen by the river, a bright bird landing) and let the recall be the CREATURE, the queen's name, or what hatches from the eggs. Match choice-shape: all four disguises real Zeus disguises (swan/bull/gold-shower/Amphitryon/eagle-for-Ganymede) -- distractors are OTHER real Zeus-disguises, not fake ones. SYMMETRIC-VOICE: told the way one would tell of Odin wandering in disguise as an old traveller, or Christ appearing in the garden as a gardener -- shapeshifting as a divine capacity. DISTRACTOR MINE: other Zeus-artifact answers (aegis vs thunderbolt vs eagle vs oak), other disguised-god seductions (Poseidon as a horse/bird), other named eagles (Prometheus's, Ganymede's -- the SAME bird in different stories).
history_overlap: GEOGRAPHY owns Olympia, Dodona and Mount Olympus as places; theology owns the temple story, the oracle story, and Zeus's court. HISTORY owns the Olympic Games as an institution; here they are the games in honour of Zeus.

name: Hera: the peacock's hundred eyes
scope: The queen of the gods and her jealousy. T1: HERA is Zeus's sister and wife, queen of Olympus, patron of marriage; her sacred bird is the PEACOCK, her sacred flower is the pomegranate, and her great temple stands at ARGOS in the Peloponnese (the Argive Heraion). T2: Zeus falls for a mortal priestess of Hera at Argos named IO; to hide her from his wife he turns her into a WHITE COW. Hera is not fooled -- she asks the cow as a gift, and Zeus, cornered, has to give it up. T3: Hera sets ARGUS PANOPTES ('the all-seeing') to guard the white cow -- a hundred-eyed GIANT who never fully sleeps because only some of his eyes close at a time (Ovid, Metamorphoses 1.622-627). T4: Zeus sends HERMES down to rescue the cow; Hermes lulls Argus asleep by playing his SHEPHERD'S PIPES and telling him the long story of the pipes' invention, until at last every eye is closed -- and Hermes strikes off his head (Metamorphoses 1.668-721). T5: Hera, mourning her watchman, takes his HUNDRED EYES and sets them into the tail-feathers of her sacred bird, the PEACOCK, where they can still be seen today (Metamorphoses 1.722-723) -- and drives Io still in cow-form all over the world with a maddening GADFLY, until she at last reaches Egypt and is restored to a woman on the banks of the Nile. Further rungs: Hera also punishes Heracles (her stepson through Alcmene) for existing -- she sends TWO SNAKES into his cradle, which the baby strangles one in each hand; Heracles's own name means 'GLORY OF HERA' because his labours are her doing; the Argive Heraion is one of the oldest large temples in the Greek world; Hera's rivalry with Aphrodite and Athena is what triggers the Trojan War when Paris awards them the golden apple.
source: PRIMARY: Ovid, Metamorphoses 1.583-750 (the whole Io / Argus / peacock cycle, esp. 1.622-627 for the hundred sleepless eyes, 1.668-721 for Hermes lulling and killing Argus, 1.722-723 for the eyes moved to the peacock's tail); Apollodorus, Bibliotheca 2.1.3 (parallel prose). Homer, Iliad 4.51-52 (Hera names her three favourite cities as Argos, Sparta and Mycenae). CONSULTED: Grokipedia 'Hera' and 'Argus Panoptes' (403; via browser 2026-09-04) and Wikipedia 'Hera', 'Io (mythology)', 'Argus Panoptes' -- Zeus's affair with Io, the white cow, Argus the hundred-eyed watchman, Hermes lulling him asleep with pipes, the eyes moved into the peacock's tail, the gadfly driving Io to Egypt, the Heraion at Argos, Heracles's cradle snakes.
framing_note: The peacock ladder -- the reveal (the EYES on the peacock's tail are Argus's) is the dinner-test hook. Dinner-test payoff: T5 (the hundred eyes on the peacock's tail are the eyes of a dead watchman-giant she loved) and T3 (Argus never fully slept because only SOME of his eyes closed at a time). ANTI-RESTATEMENT: never let the stem describe eyes on the peacock's tail AND ask what bird -- describe the SCENE (Hera mourning her dead watchman) and let the recall be the BIRD, the WATCHMAN'S NAME, or how many eyes. SYMMETRIC-VOICE: told the way one would tell of Norse Frigg weaving the fates or of the way Christian angels are described with wheels of eyes -- not 'silly primitive belief'. DISTRACTOR MINE: other Hera-sacred things (peacock vs pomegranate vs Argos), other 'hundred' beings (the Hecatoncheires, Briareus with a hundred hands -- adjacent-real, must be distinguished), other watchman-giants (Talos the bronze guardian of Crete). Wrong killer: Hermes not Apollo, not Perseus.
history_overlap: GEOGRAPHY owns Argos as a city; here it is the site of Hera's oldest temple. ANIMAL bank owns the peacock as a bird; theology owns why its tail carries eyes.

name: Poseidon and Athena: the olive and the spring
scope: The contest that gave Athens its name. T1: POSEIDON is Zeus's brother, lord of the SEA (and of horses and earthquakes); his weapon is the three-pronged TRIDENT forged for him by the Cyclopes; his sacred creature is the HORSE (he is said to have created the first horse when courting Demeter). His wife is the sea-nymph AMPHITRITE. T2: when the new city on the rock of the Acropolis was founded, two gods claimed it -- POSEIDON and ATHENA. The other Olympians made them compete: each was to give the city ONE GIFT, and the Athenians (or in some versions Kekrops the first king, or the gods themselves) would judge which gift was better (Apollodorus, Bibliotheca 3.14.1; Herodotus 8.55). T3: Poseidon struck the rock of the Acropolis with his TRIDENT and a SALT-WATER SPRING (or in Pausanias's version a well of sea-water) gushed forth -- and Pausanias says the well was still there in his day and would make a sound like waves when the south wind blew (Pausanias 1.26.5). Some versions also say a HORSE sprang out of the same strike. T4: ATHENA in her turn planted the very first OLIVE TREE, at a spot marked on the rock beside the Erechtheion -- and Pausanias again says the tree was still shown to travellers as the oldest olive in Attica. T5: the JUDGES chose the OLIVE (source of oil, wood, and food) over the salt spring, and the city was named ATHENS. Poseidon in anger flooded the plain of Attica; Athena kept the olive; the sacred olive stump was said to have burned in the Persian sack of the Acropolis in 480 BCE and to have SPROUTED a fresh shoot the very next day, which Herodotus reports as fact (Herodotus 8.55). Further rungs: Poseidon's OTHER named contest -- the fight with Athena over Troezen (judged by Zeus, awarded jointly); the trident said to be a fisherman's TUNA-SPEAR by origin, three-pronged for a reason; the sacred olive tree on the Acropolis was still tended and its oil pressed for the winners of the Panathenaic games.
source: PRIMARY: Apollodorus, Bibliotheca 3.14.1 (the contest, the trident-strike making a salt sea, Athena's olive, the vote); Herodotus 8.55 (the sacred olive on the Acropolis, its burning in 480 and its overnight regrowth); Pausanias 1.26.5 (the salt well still audible in the south wind), 1.27.2 (the sacred olive still shown). CONSULTED: Grokipedia 'Poseidon' and 'Athena' (403; via browser 2026-09-04) and Wikipedia 'Contest between Athena and Poseidon', 'Erechtheion' -- trident-strike giving the salt spring (and in some versions a horse), Athena planting the first olive, the city named Athens after her, Poseidon flooding Attica in anger, the sacred olive on the Acropolis, Herodotus's overnight regrowth after 480 BCE. CORROBORATE AT BUILD: whether Pausanias says 'well' or 'sea' at 1.26.5, whether the horse-from-trident variant is Servius or Vergil.
framing_note: The contest ladder -- the dinner-test hook is the SIMPLICITY of Athena's winning gift (an olive tree beats a saltwater spring). Dinner-test payoff: T4 (a TREE beat a SPRING) and T5 (the sacred olive really WAS burned by the Persians in 480 BCE and reportedly sprouted the next day -- Herodotus reports it as fact). SYMMETRIC-VOICE: told the way one would tell of the two men each offering King Solomon a claim over a child -- a wisdom-contest between rivals. DISTRACTOR MINE: other Athena-sacred things (owl, olive, aegis, spindle), other Poseidon-sacred things (horse, trident, dolphin, bull), other city-founding contests (Rome / the twins and the vultures -- Roman, different pillar). Wrong tools: not a lightning bolt (Zeus), not a bow (Artemis/Apollo).
history_overlap: GEOGRAPHY owns Athens and the Acropolis as places; theology owns the STORY of the naming and the olive. HISTORY owns the Persian sack of 480 BCE; here it is the day the sacred olive burned.

name: Athena's birth: fully armed from Zeus's head
scope: The strangest birth on Olympus, told in Hesiod's Theogony and the Homeric Hymn to Athena. T1: Zeus's FIRST wife was the Titaness METIS ('Wisdom' or 'Cunning'), who had helped him vomit-up his siblings; when she was pregnant with Athena, Zeus was warned by Gaia and Ouranos that any son by Metis would overthrow him just as he had overthrown his father. His solution: he SWALLOWED METIS whole while she was still pregnant (Theogony 886-900). T2: some time later he began to suffer a splitting HEADACHE unlike anything the gods had known. T3: he called HEPHAESTUS (or in some versions Prometheus) to crack his skull open with a bronze AXE (or a wedge, depending on the source) to relieve the pain. T4: when the skull opened, ATHENA sprang out FULLY GROWN and FULLY ARMED, wearing helm and breastplate and shaking her spear -- and the Homeric Hymn to Athena says all Olympus shook and the sea heaved and the sun stood still in his chariot until she took the war-gear off (Homeric Hymn 28). T5: she becomes the goddess of WISDOM AND WAR-CRAFT (as against Ares who is war-fury); her attributes are the SPEAR, the AEGIS (which she often carries for Zeus with the Gorgon-head her hero Perseus brought her), the OWL of Athens, and the SHIELD; and Metis is said to still live inside Zeus, giving him her wisdom from within (Theogony 900). Further rungs: the axe-wielder is Hephaestus in most sources but Prometheus in the older versions; the Homeric Hymn to Athena (Hymn 28) is the earliest complete narrative of the birth-scene; Athena's epithet 'Tritogeneia' ('born by the river Triton' in some versions, 'thrice-born' in others) refers to this birth; she is the CHASTE goddess who never marries, in deliberate contrast to Hera and Aphrodite.
source: PRIMARY: Hesiod, Theogony 886-900 (Zeus swallowing Metis while pregnant; Athena inside him); Homeric Hymn 28 to Athena (the birth from Zeus's head, all Olympus shaking, the sun's chariot standing still); Pindar, Olympian 7.35 (Hephaestus with the axe). Apollodorus, Bibliotheca 1.3.6 (parallel prose). CONSULTED: Grokipedia 'Athena' and 'Metis (mythology)' (403; via browser 2026-09-04) and Wikipedia 'Athena', 'Metis (mythology)' -- Metis as Zeus's first wife, the prophecy about a son overthrowing him, Zeus swallowing Metis while she was pregnant, headache, Hephaestus (or Prometheus) with the axe, Athena springing out fully armed. CORROBORATE AT BUILD: exact wording of the Homeric Hymn 28 lines about the sun standing still.
framing_note: The BIZARRE-BIRTH ladder -- the wonder is exactly how weird it is (swallowed mother, headache, axe, adult with a spear). Dinner-test payoff: T4 (she came out of his HEAD, FULLY GROWN, IN ARMOUR) and T1 (he SWALLOWED HER MOTHER first while the mother was pregnant with her). SYMMETRIC-VOICE: told the way one would tell of Dionysus reborn from Zeus's thigh, or of Christ born of Mary without a father, or of Blodeuwedd conjured from flowers -- a birth outside ordinary birth. DISTRACTOR MINE: other bizarre births (Dionysus from the thigh, Aphrodite from the sea-foam, Erichthonius from the earth), other axe-wielders (Perseus, Theseus), other swallowed goddesses. Wrong mothers: not Leto (that is Artemis and Apollo), not Semele (that is Dionysus).
history_overlap: GEOGRAPHY owns Athens; here Athena is why the city bears her name. HISTORY owns the Parthenon as building; here it is the temple to the goddess born fully armed.

name: Apollo at Delphi: the Python and the Pythia
scope: How Apollo took over the oracle at Delphi. T1: APOLLO is the son of Zeus and the Titaness LETO, twin brother of ARTEMIS; his mother had wandered the earth in labour finding no land that would take her, chased by Hera's jealousy, until the floating island of DELOS anchored itself for her, and there under a palm tree she bore first Artemis, then (with Artemis as midwife to her own brother) Apollo. T2: as a young god Apollo went hunting a great female SERPENT (or dragon) called PYTHON, which had been sent by Hera to torment his mother; the beast lived in a rocky chasm at DELPHI on the slopes of Mount PARNASSUS. Apollo shot her dead with his silver bow and buried her body in the chasm -- and the very name PYTHON comes from the Greek 'pytho', 'to rot', for her body rotting in the earth (Homeric Hymn to Apollo 300-374). T3: Apollo took the site over as his own oracle and set his PRIESTESS there, the PYTHIA -- named after the dead serpent -- who sat on a bronze TRIPOD directly over the chasm, chewed LAUREL leaves (Apollo's sacred plant) and breathed in a sweet vapour rising from the rocks; through her, in trance, Apollo answered questions. Above the entrance were carved the two mottoes 'KNOW THYSELF' (gnothi seauton) and 'NOTHING TO EXCESS' (meden agan). T4: the oracle became the most powerful in the Greek world -- Greek cities and foreign kings sent gifts, and every four years the PYTHIAN GAMES were held at Delphi in Apollo's honour, the second-oldest of the Greek games. Croesus of Lydia, planning war on Persia, sent to ask Apollo what would happen; the Pythia answered that if he crossed the river Halys he would DESTROY A GREAT EMPIRE -- he did, and the empire destroyed was his own (Herodotus 1.53). T5: to atone for the killing of Python, Apollo had to serve as a HERDSMAN for the mortal king ADMETUS for a term of years -- a god as a servant -- and the funeral games he founded FOR PYTHON became the Pythian Games. In one variant the priestess's name of PYTHIA is DIRECTLY the she-monster's own name reused as an office title -- the killer's mouth taking the victim's name. Further rungs: Apollo also carries a golden LYRE (bought or received from Hermes); the Charioteer of Delphi bronze survives from the sanctuary; the omphalos stone (Cronus's swallowed stone) was housed here; the temple's inscription 'know thyself' will be a founding text for Greek philosophy from Socrates onward.
source: PRIMARY: Homeric Hymn 3 to Apollo, esp. lines 300-374 (the killing of Python at Delphi, naming after 'pytho' to rot, the founding of the oracle); Herodotus 1.53 (Croesus and the 'great empire' answer); Pausanias 10.24 (the sanctuary, the omphalos, the two mottoes over the door). name: Artemis and Actaeon: torn by his own hounds
scope: The huntress goddess and the punishment of a peeping hunter. T1: ARTEMIS is the twin sister of Apollo, daughter of Zeus and Leto, born first on Delos (and then according to some versions midwife to her own brother the next day); she is goddess of the HUNT, the WILD, and virgin CHASTITY; her weapon is the silver BOW (a gift from the Cyclopes in some versions), her sacred animal is the DEER, and she runs in the mountains with a company of nymphs. T2: a young Theban prince and hunter named ACTAEON, out on Mount CITHAERON with his pack of fifty hunting HOUNDS, wanders through a valley called Gargaphie and by accident stumbles into a glade where a spring falls into a hollow -- and Artemis and her nymphs are BATHING (Ovid, Metamorphoses 3.155-193). T3: Artemis, mortally offended that a mortal man has seen her bare, has no bow to hand and no arrow -- she scoops UP WATER from the pool and flings it into his face, and as the droplets hit him she calls out 'now tell it, if you can tell it, that you saw Artemis bathing!' (Metamorphoses 3.192-193). T4: Actaeon feels his ears lengthen, his neck grow long, his hands become hooves -- he has been turned into a STAG. He tries to shout to his own hounds but only a stag's bell comes out. T5: his own PACK OF FIFTY HOUNDS, catching sight of a stag, run him down -- Ovid names them by name, thirty-six of them, in a hunter's-list roll-call (Metamorphoses 3.206-225): Melampus, Ichnobates, Pamphagus, Dorceus, Oribasus, Nebrophonos, Laelaps ... and they tear their own master to pieces while his hunt-companions come up shouting for Actaeon to hurry, why is he missing the kill. Further rungs: Artemis is also the goddess of childbirth (she was born painlessly and helped her mother deliver Apollo); her most famous temple, the ARTEMISION at EPHESUS, was one of the Seven Wonders of the ancient world (burnt down by Herostratus on the night Alexander the Great was born); the Roman name for her is DIANA.

Callimachus, Hymn 5 (Bath of Pallas) parallels the story with Teiresias. name: Hermes the newborn: stealing Apollo's cattle
scope: The trickster god's first day on earth, told in the Homeric Hymn to Hermes. T1: HERMES is the son of Zeus and the mountain-nymph MAIA, born in a cave on Mount CYLLENE in Arcadia; his mother lays him in his cradle and expects him to sleep. He is the messenger of the gods, guide of souls to the underworld, patron of travellers, merchants, and thieves; his gear is the WINGED SANDALS, the winged HAT (petasos), and the herald's staff CADUCEUS (Greek kerykeion) with two serpents entwined around it (a gift from Apollo). T2: on the very MORNING he is born, Hermes climbs out of his cradle, walks to the mouth of the cave, and finds a TORTOISE crawling by; he kills it, scoops out the flesh, and invents the LYRE by stretching seven cow-gut strings across the empty tortoise-shell (Homeric Hymn 4.24-61). He plays it, sings a little song, and sets it aside. T3: still on the same day, he crosses over the mountains to PIERIA in Thessaly, where his elder brother APOLLO keeps a herd of sacred CATTLE, and STEALS FIFTY OF THEM. To fool any tracker he drives them BACKWARDS so their hoof-prints point the wrong way, and puts oversized SANDALS OF TAMARISK AND MYRTLE-TWIGS on his own feet so his prints do not read as those of a baby (Homeric Hymn 4.75-86). T4: Apollo comes hunting his stolen cattle and eventually tracks the impossible trail back to the cave on Cyllene; he finds a tiny baby in a cradle who insists innocently he is far too small to have stolen any cattle -- and when Apollo drags him to Olympus for judgment, Zeus laughs at the sight of his infant son's cheek. T5: to make peace, Hermes takes out the TORTOISE-SHELL LYRE and plays it -- Apollo, god of music, is so charmed that he TRADES the whole stolen HERD for the instrument (Homeric Hymn 4.418-502), and gives Hermes in return the herald's staff (later called the caduceus). From that moment the lyre becomes APOLLO'S instrument, and Hermes becomes Apollo's brother-in-arms as god of speech and messengers. Further rungs: Hermes also invents the shepherd's PIPES (syrinx) later, which he uses to lull Argus asleep for Zeus; his winged sandals are called TALARIA; his Roman name is MERCURY.
source: PRIMARY: Homeric Hymn 4 to Hermes, esp. 24-61 (killing the tortoise and making the lyre), 75-86 (driving the cattle backwards and wearing false sandals), 156-181 (Apollo tracking him back), 418-502 (the lyre-for-herd trade). Apollodorus, Bibliotheca 3.10.2 (parallel prose). framing_note: The BABY-TRICKSTER ladder -- the reveal is he does ALL of this on his FIRST DAY. Dinner-test payoff: T2 (a newborn kills a tortoise crawling past his cradle and invents the LYRE from its shell) and T3 (the same newborn steals fifty cattle from his older brother the SUN-GOD and drives them BACKWARDS to fool the tracker). ANTI-RESTATEMENT: never let the stem say 'the lyre made from a tortoise' AND ask what Hermes invented; describe the SCENE (a baby crawling out of his cradle on the first day, a passing tortoise, elder brother's cattle in the meadow) and let the recall be the INSTRUMENT, the ANIMAL, or the trade (the lyre BOUGHT the cattle). SYMMETRIC-VOICE: told with the same warmth as Loki's tricks in Snorri, or Robin Hood's arrow-splitting -- delight, not moralism. DISTRACTOR MINE: other invented instruments (Pan's pipes / syrinx -- also invented by Hermes later but Pan's more famous; Marsyas's flute), other trickster babies (Heracles strangling snakes in the cradle), other cattle-thefts (Cacus stealing from Heracles, Autolycus stealing from Sisyphus).
history_overlap: GEOGRAPHY owns Mount Cyllene in Arcadia; here it is Hermes's birthplace cave. ANIMAL bank owns the tortoise; theology owns why its shell became a musical instrument.

name: Aphrodite born from the sea-foam
scope: The oldest and strangest birth-scene of any Olympian, told plainly in Hesiod. T1: at the very beginning of the Titan generation, CRONUS castrates his father OURANOS with a jagged sickle of adamant (a story shared with the Titanomachy ladder). Gaia had asked one of her Titan sons to do it, and only Cronus took the sickle up. T2: he flings the severed part into the SEA off the coast of the island of CYTHERA (some versions Cyprus). Where it falls, a WHITE FOAM (Greek 'aphros' -- source of the name) begins to spread across the water. T3: out of the foam rises a FULL-GROWN GODDESS, tall and beautiful, standing on a SCALLOP-SHELL (in some versions a cockle-shell) -- APHRODITE, goddess of love and desire (Theogony 188-206). She is blown by the west wind ZEPHYR onto the shore of Cyprus, and where her feet touch the ground GRASS AND FLOWERS spring up. T4: this is the origin of two of her titles -- APHRODITE URANIA ('Heavenly', because she came from Ouranos alone with no mother) and APHRODITE CYPROGENES ('Cyprus-born'). The scene is what Botticelli painted a thousand-eight hundred years later in his 'BIRTH OF VENUS' -- Venus on the shell, blown ashore by the winds, receiving her cloak. T5: at Olympus she is married off (by Zeus, or by Hera) to HEPHAESTUS the smith -- a match considered ridiculous by the other gods, the most beautiful to the ugliest -- and takes ARES the war god as her lover. Her attendants are the three GRACES (Charites) and EROS (Cupid), her sacred bird is the DOVE, her sacred flower is the ROSE, her weapon is a magic GIRDLE (kestos) that makes anyone who sees her wearing it fall in love -- Hera borrows it once in the Iliad to seduce Zeus (Iliad 14.214-217). Further rungs: an alternative genealogy in Homer makes her simply the daughter of Zeus and DIONE (Iliad 5.370) -- so 'foam-born' is Hesiod's version and 'Zeus's daughter' is Homer's; the western wind that blows her ashore is Zephyr, one of the four cardinal winds; her Roman name is VENUS.
source: PRIMARY: Hesiod, Theogony 188-206 (the castration, the fall into the sea, the foam, the birth of Aphrodite, the naming from 'aphros', Cythera and Cyprus, grass and flowers under her feet); Homeric Hymn 6 to Aphrodite (Zephyr carrying her to Cyprus, the Hours dressing her); Homer, Iliad 5.370-417 (Aphrodite as Zeus's daughter by Dione -- alternate lineage), 14.214-217 (the girdle). CONSULTED: Grokipedia 'Aphrodite' (403; via browser 2026-09-04) and Wikipedia 'Aphrodite', 'Birth of Venus (Botticelli)' -- born from the sea-foam where Ouranos's severed part fell, near Cythera, blown by Zephyr to Cyprus, married to Hephaestus, lover of Ares, dove/rose/girdle, Botticelli's 1485 painting. CORROBORATE AT BUILD: whether the shell is scallop, cockle, or unnamed in the earliest sources (Botticelli's shell is Renaissance iconography).
framing_note: The FOAM-BIRTH ladder -- the reveal is that 'Aphrodite' literally means 'from foam' and the foam is from Ouranos's SEVERED PART falling into the sea. Dinner-test payoff: T3 (she rose out of SEA-FOAM, an adult, on a shell) and T2 (the foam is from what Cronus threw into the sea after cutting his father). ANTI-RESTATEMENT: never let the stem say 'foam-born' AND ask who; describe the SCENE (a severed thing falling into the sea, foam spreading, a full-grown goddess rising) and let the recall be the GODDESS, the origin of the FOAM, or the ISLAND. SYMMETRIC-VOICE: told the way one would tell of any myth's origin-of-a-god scene -- Athena from the head, Dionysus from the thigh, Christ born of a virgin. Weird divine birth is a divine-birth pattern. DISTRACTOR MINE: other strange births (Athena / Dionysus / Erichthonius), other 'born from the sea' figures (Amphitrite, Thetis -- adjacent-real sea-goddesses), Aphrodite's alternate lineage (Zeus and Dione, the Homer version -- accept both, don't confuse). Botticelli belongs on the frame, not as the origin.
history_overlap: GEOGRAPHY owns Cyprus and Cythera as places; here they are the two candidate landing-shores for a goddess. Art history owns Botticelli's Uffizi painting; theology owns why he painted her on a shell.

name: Ares reviled: the war god the gods hate
scope: The Olympian nobody actually likes. T1: ARES is the son of Zeus and Hera, one of the twelve Olympians, god of WAR -- but specifically of war-fury, slaughter, and the joy of killing (as against Athena, who is war-CRAFT). His attendants in battle are his sons DEIMOS ('Terror') and PHOBOS ('Fear'), and the goddess ENYO the sacker-of-cities; his sacred animals are the vulture and the wild boar. T2: he is the LEAST popular god on Olympus. In the Iliad, Zeus tells him to his face -- 'To me thou art most hateful of all the gods that hold Olympus: for ever strife is dear to thee and wars and battles' (Iliad 5.890-891). T3: he is wounded in the Iliad by the mortal hero DIOMEDES (with Athena's help) and runs bleeding back to Olympus to complain -- Homer says his cry as he was struck was 'like nine or ten thousand men shouting in battle' (Iliad 5.859-863); his father tells him he deserved it. T4: he is also caught in Hephaestus's famous BRONZE-NET TRAP with Aphrodite (see the Hephaestus ladder) -- naked, tangled, and laughed at by every god summoned to witness the scene. T5: in worship he was a NORTHERN god, more honoured among the wild Thracians and the Scythians than among the Greeks proper; the Romans, by contrast, elevated their equivalent MARS to father-of-Romulus, ancestor of the whole race -- so Rome's war-god is dignified where Greece's is despised. Further rungs: Ares's children include (besides Deimos and Phobos) the war-horse-taming Diomedes of Thrace (whom Heracles later killed by feeding him to his own mares); the AREOPAGUS ('Ares's Hill') in Athens is where he was said to have stood trial for the killing of Poseidon's son Halirrhothius -- the first murder trial ever held.
source: PRIMARY: Homer, Iliad 5.827-909 (Ares wounded by Diomedes with Athena's help, his shout like ten thousand men, running to Olympus to complain, Zeus rebuking him at 5.890-891); Odyssey 8.266-366 (the net-trap with Aphrodite -- see Hephaestus ladder); Apollodorus, Bibliotheca 3.14.2 (trial on the Areopagus for killing Halirrhothius). CONSULTED: Grokipedia 'Ares' (403; via browser 2026-09-04) and Wikipedia 'Ares' -- Olympian son of Zeus and Hera, war-fury vs Athena's war-craft, Deimos and Phobos, wounded by Diomedes, shout like ten thousand, net-trap with Aphrodite, Areopagus trial, Thracian and Scythian cult, contrast with Roman Mars. CORROBORATE AT BUILD: verify Iliad 5.890-891 quote wording from a standard translation before locking a quote-recall rung.
framing_note: The UNPOPULAR-GOD ladder -- the reveal is that the war-god is the gods' LEAST-LIKED member. Dinner-test payoff: T2 (his own FATHER tells him 'to me thou art most hateful of all the gods') and T3 (a MORTAL hero wounded him and he ran home crying, and Zeus told him he had it coming). ANTI-RESTATEMENT: never let the stem say 'war god' and then ask his name -- describe the SCENE (a god shouting like ten thousand men, running wounded back to Olympus to complain to his father) and let the recall be the GOD, or the mortal who wounded him, or what his father said. SYMMETRIC-VOICE: told the way one would tell of Loki being bound and reviled at the end of the Aesir's feast, or of Cain marked and set apart -- a divine figure held at a distance BY the divine. DISTRACTOR MINE: other war-figures (Athena as war-craft, the Roman Mars, the Norse Tyr, Enyo, Bellona), other wounded gods (Aphrodite in the same Iliad passage, cut by Diomedes on the wrist), other 'hated' gods (Hades disliked by his siblings). name: Hephaestus: thrown from Olympus, the throne trap, the shield
scope: The smith-god of Olympus and his three signature stories. T1: HEPHAESTUS is the son of Hera (in some versions by Zeus, in others by Hera alone in jealousy at Zeus's Athena-birth); he is the divine SMITH, master of the FORGE under Mount Etna (or under the Aegean island of LEMNOS) where the CYCLOPES work as his assistants. He is the only Olympian who is LAME. T2: the reason for his lameness has two versions -- in one, Hera bore him so ugly and misshapen that she THREW HIM OUT of Olympus herself in disgust, and he fell for a whole day into the sea, where the sea-nymphs Thetis and Eurynome caught and raised him (Iliad 18.394-405, from Hephaestus's own mouth); in the other, Zeus threw him out for taking Hera's side in a quarrel, and he fell for a whole day and landed on Lemnos, breaking his leg (Iliad 1.590-594). Both stories are IN the Iliad, told in different books. T3: in revenge for being cast out, Hephaestus forges a beautiful GOLDEN THRONE and sends it to Hera as a peace-offering; when she sits down on it, INVISIBLE CHAINS spring up and TRAP HER, and no god can undo them. The other Olympians beg him to come up and free his mother, and only DIONYSUS is able to persuade him -- by getting him drunk on wine, sitting him on the back of a MULE (or donkey), and leading him back up to Olympus in a comic procession (a scene painted on hundreds of Greek vases as 'The Return of Hephaestus'). T4: married off (as compensation) to APHRODITE, he finds her sleeping with Ares; he forges a NET SO FINE it is invisible, drops it over the two of them in bed, and SUMMONS THE OTHER GODS to come and see -- the male Olympians roar with laughter, Poseidon awkwardly negotiates the couple's release, Aphrodite flees for Cyprus in shame, Ares slinks off to Thrace (Odyssey 8.266-366). T5: his masterpiece is the SHIELD OF ACHILLES, forged in a single night at Thetis's request when Achilles's own armour has been stripped from Patroclus's corpse -- the whole shield covered with scenes of the earth, sea, and sky, two cities (one at peace, one at war), a wedding, a court trial, harvests, dances, and the ocean encircling all (Iliad 18.478-608). Homer describes the shield for over 130 lines -- the founding piece of Greek 'ekphrasis' (poetic description of art). Further rungs: also forges the CHARIOT OF THE SUN for Helios, the necklace of HARMONIA (which brings doom to whoever wears it), the automatons that assist him at the forge (bronze women who move and speak -- Iliad 18.417-421); his Roman name is VULCAN and it is Vulcan whose forge under Etna makes the volcano smoke.
source: PRIMARY: Homer, Iliad 1.590-594 (thrown out by Zeus, day-long fall, landing on Lemnos), 18.394-405 (thrown out by Hera his mother, caught by Thetis and Eurynome, both versions in Homer), 18.478-608 (the making of Achilles's shield -- founding ekphrasis), 18.417-421 (bronze automaton-women at the forge); Odyssey 8.266-366 (net-trap of Ares and Aphrodite). Apollodorus, Bibliotheca 1.3.5 (Hera born him alone in jealousy). The golden-throne / return-drunk story: Alcaeus fr. 349, Pausanias 1.20.3, and hundreds of Attic vases. framing_note: The three-signature-scenes ladder -- keep the fall / throne / shield beats distinct, don't let them blur. Dinner-test payoff: T3 (he forged an INVISIBLE-CHAIN throne to trap his own mother in revenge, and only DIONYSUS could talk him into freeing her -- by getting him drunk on a donkey) and T4 (he caught his wife with Ares in a NET and called all the gods in to watch). ANTI-RESTATEMENT: never let the stem describe the invisible net AND ask who made it; describe the SCENE (a lame smith, a magic net over a bed, laughing gods) and let the recall be the SMITH, or the throne trap's target (his own mother), or Dionysus as the one who brought him back. Choice parity: for the shield-of-Achilles rung, distractors are OTHER named divine artifacts (Zeus's aegis, Athena's owl, Poseidon's trident). SYMMETRIC-VOICE: told the way one would tell of Wayland the Smith in Norse and Anglo-Saxon lore or of Sindri and Brokkr forging Mjolnir -- a divine smith as maker of impossible things. DISTRACTOR MINE: other cast-out gods (Kronos in Tartarus, Prometheus on the crag), other 'shield' scenes (the Shield of Herakles attributed to Hesiod, Aeneas's shield in Vergil -- adjacent-real ekphrasis).

name: Dionysus: twice-born, the pirates, the maenads
scope: The wine-god, born twice and revenging himself on those who deny him. T1: DIONYSUS is the son of Zeus and the Theban princess SEMELE, daughter of King CADMUS; jealous Hera, disguised as an old nurse, whispers to Semele that her lover might not really be a god -- and persuades her to ask Zeus to appear to her in his true form. Zeus has sworn any oath Semele demands, so he must; and when he appears in his lightning-glory, Semele is burned to death on the spot (Ovid, Metamorphoses 3.259-315). T2: Zeus, moving fast, snatches the unborn baby from her burning womb and SEWS HIM INTO HIS OWN THIGH -- and carries him there until he is ready to be born, months later, out of the thigh. This is the FIRST birth ('once from Semele, once from the thigh' -- hence the epithet DITHYRAMBUS 'twice-born'). T3: grown up, he introduces the vine to mortals and travels with a wild retinue -- the MAENADS ('raving women') dressed in fawnskins, carrying the THYRSUS (a fennel-stalk topped with a pine-cone, wound with ivy), and the goat-legged SATYRS with their leader SILENUS on a donkey. In Euripides's Bacchae, the king of Thebes PENTHEUS refuses to accept the new god's rites; Dionysus lets Pentheus be caught spying on the maenads on Mount CITHAERON, and Pentheus's own mother AGAVE, in bacchic frenzy, tears him limb from limb, believing he is a mountain lion, and returns to the city with his head on her thyrsus. T4: sailing across the sea one day disguised as a young man, Dionysus is captured by TYRRHENIAN PIRATES who plan to sell him as a slave -- only the helmsman recognises him as a god and begs them to let him go. As the ship puts out, VINES sprout from the mast and cover the rigging, WINE runs across the deck, the oars turn into SERPENTS, and Dionysus himself takes the form of a LION on the deck; the terrified pirates leap overboard and are turned into DOLPHINS -- all except the good helmsman, who is spared (Homeric Hymn 7 to Dionysus). T5: he goes down into the UNDERWORLD to bring his mortal mother SEMELE back up -- one of the very few successful underworld-descents in Greek myth -- and settles her on Olympus under the name THYONE; he then marries the abandoned Cretan princess ARIADNE on the island of NAXOS after she has been left there by Theseus, and sets her bridal crown as a constellation in the sky (the CORONA BOREALIS). Further rungs: Dionysus is the god of the theatre -- the Great Dionysia festival at Athens is where Greek tragedy is born; his other epithets include BACCHUS (Roman name and general Greek); his sacred plant is the vine and the ivy; his sacred animals are the leopard, the bull, and the goat.
source: PRIMARY: Ovid, Metamorphoses 3.259-315 (Semele's burning); Euripides, Bacchae (the whole Pentheus scene, esp. 1043-1152 for Agave tearing her son); Homeric Hymn 7 to Dionysus (the pirates, vines up the mast, wine on the deck, dolphins); Hesiod, Theogony 940-942 (Semele bearing him). name: Demeter and Persephone: the pomegranate seeds
scope: The mother-daughter story that explains winter, told in the Homeric Hymn to Demeter. T1: DEMETER is the older sister of Zeus, goddess of GRAIN and the harvest; her daughter PERSEPHONE (also called Kore, 'the Maiden'), whom she has by Zeus, is her only child. One day Persephone is gathering FLOWERS in a meadow at NYSA (or Enna in Sicily in the Roman version); she reaches to pluck an especially beautiful NARCISSUS that Gaia has grown as a lure. T2: the earth splits open and HADES, lord of the dead, rises in a black chariot drawn by four immortal HORSES, seizes Persephone, and carries her down into the underworld to be his queen -- with Zeus's silent consent (Homeric Hymn 2.1-32). No one sees but HELIOS the sun and HECATE the goddess of the crossroads. T3: Demeter wanders the earth for nine days and nights, torch in hand, searching for her daughter and finding no trace; she takes the form of an OLD WOMAN and comes to the town of ELEUSIS, where she is welcomed by the royal family and nurses the baby prince DEMOPHOON, whom she tries to make immortal by holding him in the FIRE at night (she is caught by his mother and stops). She then reveals her true form and orders a temple built at Eleusis in her honour (Hymn 2.185-274). T4: still furious, Demeter blights the earth -- NO GRAIN grows for a whole year, the plow-oxen pull at the plows in vain, mortals are starving and the gods are getting no sacrifices, and Zeus finally has to intervene. He sends HERMES down to fetch Persephone back. But Hades has slyly given her SIX POMEGRANATE SEEDS to eat (some versions six, some four, some three) -- and anyone who has eaten in the underworld cannot fully leave (Hymn 2.371-404). T5: the compromise: Persephone spends ONE THIRD OF THE YEAR (or in some versions half, matching the number of seeds) below with Hades as queen of the dead, and the rest above with her mother. When she is below Demeter grieves and the earth withers -- and this is WINTER; when she comes back up in spring the grain rises again. Demeter gives the Eleusinians in gratitude the ELEUSINIAN MYSTERIES, the initiation rites held at Eleusis for over a thousand years, whose secret is famously never written down (Hymn 2.470-489). Further rungs: TRIPTOLEMOS the Eleusinian prince learns from Demeter how to grow grain, is given a winged serpent-drawn chariot, and flies over the world teaching agriculture; the number of pomegranate seeds is variously 3 / 4 / 6 across sources (the Hymn does not give a number).

Ovid, Metamorphoses 5.341-571 (parallel version, sets it at Enna in Sicily); Apollodorus, Bibliotheca 1.5. name: Hades and the underworld: Cerberus, Styx, Charon
scope: The Greek underworld and its geography. T1: HADES is Zeus's brother, third of the three lot-drawing brothers (Zeus sky, Poseidon sea, Hades underworld); his kingdom is the LAND OF THE DEAD, deep beneath the earth (the Greeks came to call the whole realm 'Hades' as well); his queen is PERSEPHONE, whom he abducted; his helmet is the CAP OF INVISIBILITY (kynee) forged for him by the Cyclopes, and he lends it to gods and heroes (Athena wears it in the Iliad, Perseus wears it to approach Medusa). T2: the entrance is guarded by CERBERUS, the THREE-HEADED DOG (in Hesiod's Theogony 311 he actually has FIFTY heads, but the standard iconography settles on three); he has a mane of live SNAKES down his back and a serpent for a tail. He fawns on those coming IN and rages at any soul trying to leave. The souls that make it past are ferried across the RIVER of the underworld by CHARON, the grim old ferryman, who demands one small bronze COIN (obol) placed under the tongue at burial for passage; those who cannot pay are turned back and wander the shore for a hundred years. T3: the FIVE RIVERS of the underworld each have a role -- STYX (the river of hatred/oath, ringed nine times around the underworld, and the river by whose waters even the gods swear their unbreakable oaths), ACHERON (the river of woe -- the one Charon actually ferries across, in most sources), COCYTUS (the river of lamentation), PHLEGETHON (the river of FIRE), and LETHE (the river of FORGETFULNESS, whose water souls drink to forget their old lives before returning above in reincarnation, in Plato's Republic 10). T4: three JUDGES of the dead sit at a crossroads -- MINOS (former king of Crete), his brother RHADAMANTHYS, and AEACUS (grandfather of Achilles) -- and they route each newly-arrived soul to one of three destinations. T5: three DESTINATIONS -- the FIELDS OF ASPHODEL (grey neutral meadows for the ordinary dead), the pit of TARTARUS deep below (for the wicked and the imprisoned Titans, where Sisyphus rolls, Tantalus thirsts, and the Titans are chained), and the ELYSIAN FIELDS at the western edge (where heroes and the pure go, sunlit and warm). Further rungs: the WHITE POPLAR is Hades's sacred tree (Persephone weaves a wreath of it); the underworld has an ADAMANTINE GATE that Cerberus guards; the pomegranate is Hades's fruit through Persephone; Hades is also called PLOUTON ('the Rich One') because gold and gems come from beneath the earth -- his Roman name Pluto keeps this meaning; the Greeks avoided saying 'Hades' aloud out of superstition and used the epithet instead.

name: Prometheus: fire in the fennel-stalk, the eagle at the liver
scope: The Titan who chose mortals over the gods. T1: PROMETHEUS ('Forethought') is a Titan of the second generation, son of the Titan Iapetos; his three brothers include EPIMETHEUS ('Afterthought', who marries Pandora and takes her jar), MENOETIUS (thrown down into Tartarus by Zeus), and ATLAS (holding up the sky). In the Titanomachy he sides WITH Zeus against the older Titans and so keeps his freedom afterwards. T2: at MECONE (an ancient place in Greek Sikyon), Prometheus is asked to divide a sacrificial OX into two portions -- one for the gods, one for mortals. He wraps the BONES in a shining coat of FAT so they look richer, and hides the meat and offal inside the ugly ox-stomach. Zeus, offered the choice, picks the fat-covered pile and finds the bones underneath -- and from that day mortals get to eat the meat and gods get only the burnt fat-and-bones smoke at every sacrifice (Hesiod, Theogony 535-560). T3: in fury Zeus denies mortals FIRE. Prometheus goes up (or across) to Olympus, steals a spark, and carries it down to earth hidden inside a hollow FENNEL-STALK -- the pithy inside of a giant fennel smoulders for days like a slow match, so a spark can be carried in it invisibly (Theogony 565-569). T4: as further punishment for mortals, Zeus has Hephaestus fashion the first woman, PANDORA (see the Pandora ladder), and sends her with a JAR to Prometheus's foolish brother Epimetheus -- who accepts her against Prometheus's warning. Meanwhile, Zeus has Prometheus himself CHAINED to a crag in the CAUCASUS mountains at the edge of the world, and sends an EAGLE (Zeus's own bird) to tear out his LIVER every day; the liver GROWS BACK every night, so the torture is eternal (Theogony 521-525). T5: centuries later, HERACLES, passing through the Caucasus on one of his labours, sees the eagle at the crag and SHOOTS IT with an arrow; he then persuades Zeus to leave Prometheus freed. In the version told in Aeschylus's Prometheus Bound, Prometheus also holds a SECRET -- the name of the mother by whom Zeus is fated to father a son greater than himself -- and it is by threatening to reveal this that he eventually wins his release. Further rungs: in Ovid and later versions Prometheus is ALSO the creator of the first humans, moulding them from CLAY and water (Metamorphoses 1.82-83); the fennel-stalk (Greek 'narthex') is a real Mediterranean plant with a pithy hollow interior used in classical times as an actual firebrand-carrier; his name 'Prometheus' ('forethought') is set against his brother 'Epimetheus' ('afterthought') as the smart brother and the fool.
source: PRIMARY: Hesiod, Theogony 521-616 (the chaining, the eagle at the liver, Mecone with the bones-under-fat trick, fire in the fennel-stalk); Works and Days 42-105 (Prometheus's theft and the sending of Pandora); Aeschylus, Prometheus Bound (whole play, esp. the secret about Zeus's fated son); Ovid, Metamorphoses 1.82-83 (Prometheus as clay-moulder of humankind). Dinner-test payoff: T3 (he hid the STOLEN SPARK inside a hollow FENNEL-STALK to carry it down to earth) and T4 (Zeus's own EAGLE ate his LIVER every day and it grew back every night, until HERACLES shot it). SYMMETRIC-VOICE: told the way one would tell of Loki bound with his son's entrails under a serpent's venom in Snorri, or of Christ bearing the cross to Golgotha -- a suffering-figure whose torment carries a specific concrete image. DISTRACTOR MINE: other Titan-punishments (Atlas holding the sky, Cronus in Tartarus), other bound sufferers (Ixion on the wheel, Sisyphus at the boulder -- adjacent-real, both in the punishment strand), other 'stolen' things (fire vs the Golden Fleece vs Cerberus vs the apples of the Hesperides). Wrong bird: not a vulture (that is Tityos), not a hawk -- an EAGLE.
history_overlap: GEOGRAPHY owns the Caucasus as a mountain range; here they are the crag where a Titan was chained. PHILOSOPHY owns the story as an ethical fable about defiance of authority; theology owns the story as story (the Titan, the fennel-stalk, the liver, the eagle).

name: Atlas holding up the sky: the trick Heracles played
scope: The Titan who lost the war and got the world for a burden. T1: ATLAS is a second-generation Titan, brother of Prometheus and Epimetheus, son of the Titan Iapetos and the Oceanid Clymene. In the Titanomachy he sides with the OLD Titans against Zeus, and fights on the losing side. T2: when Zeus punishes the defeated Titans by casting them into Tartarus, Atlas alone is given a different fate -- he is condemned to stand at the WESTERN EDGE OF THE WORLD and hold up the SKY (the ouranos, the vault of heaven, not the earth -- classical depictions of Atlas carrying the round earth on his shoulders are a Renaissance MISREADING) forever on his shoulders (Theogony 517-520). His station is the far west of the Mediterranean, and the mountain range in modern Morocco called the ATLAS MOUNTAINS is named for him -- travellers said the range was Atlas himself turned to stone. T3: the ELEVENTH LABOUR of HERACLES is to fetch the golden APPLES OF THE HESPERIDES, which grow on a tree in a garden at the western edge of the world -- guarded by the hundred-headed dragon LADON and tended by the HESPERIDES, three (or seven) nymph-daughters OF ATLAS. Heracles goes west and finds Atlas standing under his burden. T4: Heracles proposes a deal -- ATLAS is the father of the tending nymphs and can walk into the garden freely, while Heracles cannot; if Atlas will fetch the apples for him, Heracles will hold the sky in the meantime. Atlas gladly agrees, and Heracles takes the sky on his shoulders. Atlas fetches the apples and returns -- and then tries to walk off, saying he will deliver them for Heracles too, leaving Heracles holding the sky forever (Apollodorus 2.5.11). T5: Heracles, seeing the trick, pretends to agree -- he only asks that Atlas take the sky back for a moment while he arranges a PAD OF CLOTH on his shoulders to cushion the weight, since he was not expecting to hold it so long. The moment Atlas takes the sky back, Heracles picks up the apples and walks off, leaving Atlas back under his burden forever. Further rungs: Perseus, returning from killing Medusa, is said in another version to have shown the Gorgon's head to Atlas as vengeance for a refused hospitality, and turned him to STONE -- and that is the OTHER version of how the Atlas Mountains got there (Ovid, Metamorphoses 4.626-662); Atlas is also the grandfather of Odysseus through his daughter Calypso, who keeps Odysseus for seven years on Ogygia; the seven daughters of Atlas and Pleione are the PLEIADES, seven stars in the sky just above his head.
source: PRIMARY: Hesiod, Theogony 517-520 (Atlas holding up the sky at the world's edge); Apollodorus, Bibliotheca 2.5.11 (the eleventh labour of Heracles, the apple-fetching trick with Atlas); Ovid, Metamorphoses 4.626-662 (Perseus turning Atlas to stone -- alternate origin of the Atlas Mountains); Homer, Odyssey 1.52-54 (Atlas holding up the pillars that keep sky and earth apart). Wrong burden: not the earth (the Renaissance-globe iconography is later error), not a mountain.
history_overlap: GEOGRAPHY owns the Atlas Mountains as an African range and the Atlantic Ocean as a name derived from him; here they are named for the Titan. Astronomy owns the Pleiades cluster; here they are his daughters.

name: Pandora and the jar: hope alone remaining
scope: The first woman, the mistranslated jar, and the one thing left inside. T1: after PROMETHEUS steals fire in the fennel-stalk (see that ladder), Zeus wants to punish mortals a second time. He orders HEPHAESTUS to mould from clay a beautiful FIRST WOMAN, PANDORA ('All-Gifted'); ATHENA teaches her weaving and dresses her, APHRODITE gives her charm and desire, the GRACES set golden necklaces on her, HERMES gives her cunning speech and a deceitful heart, and each Olympian adds a gift -- hence her name (Works and Days 60-89). T2: Zeus sends her down as a bride to Prometheus's foolish brother EPIMETHEUS ('Afterthought'), even though Prometheus has warned Epimetheus never to accept a gift from Zeus. Epimetheus, true to his name, accepts her -- and only THEN remembers his brother's warning (Works and Days 83-89). T3: with her Pandora carries a great JAR (Greek 'pithos' -- a large ceramic storage jar, NOT a box; the word 'box' is a MISTRANSLATION by Erasmus in 1508 who rendered pithos as the Latin 'pyxis', a small box, and the mistake stuck). Inside the jar are all the EVILS -- hard labour, sickness, old age, envy, war, hunger -- that had never before troubled mortals. T4: Pandora, out of curiosity, LIFTS THE LID; the evils fly out in a swarm and scatter across the world, and can never be put back. Only ONE thing remains behind, still inside the jar under the closing lid: ELPIS ('Hope' -- or 'expectation' -- the Greek word is deliberately ambiguous), because Pandora slammed the lid back on JUST IN TIME (Works and Days 90-104). T5: what Hope being left INSIDE the jar means is famously disputed even in antiquity -- is Hope trapped INSIDE (a good thing kept from mortals) or SAFE inside (a good thing preserved for them)? Hesiod does not say. The story is the Greek version of an origin-of-suffering myth parallel to the Genesis Fall; both feature a first woman, a forbidden object, a lid or a fruit, and the loss of a paradisal condition. Further rungs: Hesiod's Theogony version (570-612) tells the same story with slightly different emphasis (the woman as 'evil for mortals' from the start); the Roman version keeps the jar; only from the sixteenth century onward does 'Pandora's box' become the English idiom because of Erasmus.
source: PRIMARY: Hesiod, Works and Days 47-105 (the full Pandora story: made by Hephaestus, all Olympians giving gifts, sent to Epimetheus, jar opened, hope alone left); Theogony 570-612 (the parallel version). Erasmus, Adagia 1.1.31 (the 1508 mistranslation of 'pithos' as 'pyxis', origin of English 'Pandora's box'). CONSULTED: Grokipedia 'Pandora' (403; via browser 2026-09-04) and Wikipedia 'Pandora', 'Pandora's box' -- first woman, all Olympians contributing gifts, sent to Epimetheus after Zeus's warning, jar (pithos not box), lid opened, evils scattered, hope alone remaining, Erasmus 1508 mistranslation as origin of the English 'box' idiom, ambiguity of whether hope inside is trapped or saved.
framing_note: The MISTRANSLATION ladder -- the fact that it's a JAR not a BOX is a dinner-test hook adults never know. Dinner-test payoff: T3 (it was a JAR, not a box -- the 'box' is a 16th-century mistranslation by Erasmus) and T4 (of all the evils that flew out, HOPE alone stayed inside -- and Hesiod does not say whether that means hope is trapped OR safe). ANTI-RESTATEMENT: never let the stem say 'jar' AND ask what she opened -- describe the SCENE (the first woman, a sealed vessel, evils in a swarm) and let the recall be the VESSEL-TYPE, or WHO OPENED IT, or WHAT WAS LEFT. Explicit parallel to Genesis Fall is FAIR in this pillar (they are structural parallels, not derivation-claims). name: The Five Ages of Man: Gold, Silver, Bronze, Heroic, Iron
scope: Hesiod's history of the world in five ages, told in Works and Days 109-201. T1: HESIOD writes for his brother Perses a poem about honest work and just judgment; embedded in it is a myth of DECLINE across five successive ages, each named for a metal (except one). The first is the AGE OF GOLD, in the reign of Cronus -- mortals then were like gods, lived without toil, without old age, feasted in perpetual spring, and when they died they became BENEVOLENT SPIRITS ('daimones') who watch over the living. T2: the SILVER AGE follows under Zeus -- these mortals live a hundred years as children under their mothers, and only a short foolish adulthood; they refuse to sacrifice to the gods and Zeus puts them away. T3: the BRONZE AGE -- terrible warriors born from ash-trees, with bronze armour, bronze weapons, bronze tools, bronze HOUSES (Works and Days 150-151); they fought so much they wiped themselves out and went unnamed into Hades. T4: the fourth age BREAKS THE METAL PATTERN -- it is the AGE OF HEROES, more just and better than the bronze that came before, in which the great heroes of legend lived and fought at Thebes and at Troy; when they die some go down to Hades but others are sent to the ISLES OF THE BLESSED at the edge of Ocean, where Cronus is again king and grain grows three times a year for them (Works and Days 156-173). This is the age of Achilles, Ajax, Odysseus, the Argonauts. T5: the fifth and CURRENT age is the AGE OF IRON, and Hesiod says he is unhappy to be born into it -- toil and grief by day, worry by night, the gods will send new sorrows, children will dishonour parents, guests dishonour hosts, brother turn on brother, and finally the goddesses of shame (AIDOS) and righteous indignation (NEMESIS) will wrap their faces in white veils and depart from the earth to Olympus, and mortals will have no defence against evil (Works and Days 197-201). Further rungs: the schema (declining ages named for metals) is echoed and adapted -- in the biblical Book of Daniel 2.31-45 King Nebuchadnezzar's dream-statue has a head of gold, breast of silver, belly of bronze, legs of iron, and feet of iron and clay (adjacent-real, do not conflate but note parallel); in Ovid's Metamorphoses 1.89-150 the five are compressed back into four (gold / silver / bronze / iron, dropping the Heroic age).
source: PRIMARY: Hesiod, Works and Days 109-201 (the whole five-ages passage). Ovid, Metamorphoses 1.89-150 (Roman four-age simplification). Daniel 2.31-45 (Christian pillar parallel -- Nebuchadnezzar's dream). CONSULTED: Grokipedia 'Ages of Man' (403; via browser 2026-09-04) and Wikipedia 'Ages of Man' -- five ages of Hesiod (gold under Cronus / silver / bronze / heroic exception / iron the present), the golden dead becoming benevolent daimones, bronze-age warriors dwelling in bronze houses, the heroic age at Thebes and Troy with the Isles of the Blessed as afterlife, iron age ending in Aidos and Nemesis leaving the earth. framing_note: The DECLINE-of-history ladder -- the surprise is the FIFTH item (Heroic breaking the metal pattern). Dinner-test payoff: T4 (there are FIVE ages, not four -- the Heroic age breaks the metal pattern and includes Achilles and Odysseus) and T5 (Hesiod says the last age -- OURS -- ends when SHAME and NEMESIS wrap their faces and leave the earth). ANTI-RESTATEMENT: never let the stem list the metals AND ask what pattern -- describe the SCENE (a poet writing to his brother about honest work, a schema of decline) and let the recall be the ODD ONE OUT (Heroic), or the FINAL age's ending, or WHAT CHANGES in each. SYMMETRIC-VOICE: told the way one would tell of Norse Ragnarok's slow unwinding or of the Christian last-days ending, or of the Kali Yuga in Hindu thought (OUT of pillar). A world-in-decline schema. name: Deucalion and Pyrrha: stones thrown over the shoulder
scope: The Greek flood-story, close cousin to Noah. T1: at the end of the Bronze Age (in Ovid's telling, Metamorphoses 1.253-415) mortals have grown so wicked that ZEUS decides to destroy them with a great FLOOD. He forbids the north winds from blowing (which would clear the storms), calls up the south wind, and unleashes his brother POSEIDON to send the seas over the land. T2: only one couple is warned to survive -- DEUCALION, king of PHTHIA in Thessaly, son of PROMETHEUS, and his wife PYRRHA, daughter of Epimetheus and Pandora. Warned by Prometheus, Deucalion builds a wooden CHEST (or an ARK or a boat, depending on the version) and puts them both inside with provisions. T3: they float for nine days and nine nights as the flood covers all the land, and finally the chest grounds on the top of MOUNT PARNASSUS (in Ovid; other versions say Etna, Athos, Aetna, or Othrys -- but Parnassus, the twin-peaked mountain also sacred to Apollo and Delphi, is the settled canonical landing). T4: coming down from the mountain to a desolate earth, Deucalion and Pyrrha go to the oracle of THEMIS (an older goddess, before Apollo took over Delphi) and ask how to repopulate the world. The oracle answers -- 'Cover your heads, unloose your girdles, and throw behind you the BONES OF YOUR GREAT MOTHER' (Metamorphoses 1.381-383). T5: Pyrrha at first refuses in horror -- until Deucalion realises the great mother is the EARTH, and the BONES OF THE EARTH are STONES. They walk on, veiled, and toss stones back over their shoulders -- the stones DEUCALION throws become MEN and those PYRRHA throws become WOMEN, and the earth is repopulated (Metamorphoses 1.395-415). Further rungs: Deucalion is also the father of HELLEN, from whom all the HELLENES (Greeks) are descended by name; the Deucalion flood is the third of five great floods in Greek myth, and by far the best-attested; the parallel to Noah (an ark, one couple saved, a mountaintop landing, a new beginning) is close enough that some ancient writers noted it explicitly.
source: PRIMARY: Ovid, Metamorphoses 1.253-415 (the whole story: Jove's decision, the winds, Poseidon's flood, the chest, nine days, Parnassus landing, the oracle of Themis, the stones over the shoulders); Apollodorus, Bibliotheca 1.7.2 (parallel prose version); Pindar, Olympian 9.41-53 (Deucalion and Pyrrha throwing stones). name: Sisyphus: cheating Death, chaining Thanatos, the boulder
scope: The trickster king punished for outsmarting death itself, twice. T1: SISYPHUS is the founder-king of the city of CORINTH (Ephyra in the older name) and the cunningest mortal alive; he is a match for gods at trickery. In the Iliad Homer already calls him 'the most cunning of men' (Iliad 6.153). T2: the FIRST offence -- Zeus swoops down and abducts the river-nymph AEGINA. Her father the river-god ASOPUS comes searching, and Sisyphus tells him where Zeus has taken her, in exchange for Asopus giving Corinth a spring of fresh water (Peirene, still famous in classical times). Zeus, furious at being told on, sends THANATOS ('Death' personified) to fetch Sisyphus down to the underworld in chains. T3: Sisyphus, ready for him, asks Thanatos to DEMONSTRATE how the chains work -- and when Thanatos puts them on to show, Sisyphus locks him in and hides him in a cupboard. With DEATH bound in a Corinthian cupboard, NO ONE ON EARTH CAN DIE -- old people cannot die, wounded soldiers cannot die, the sick cannot die; Ares the war god comes down enraged that no one dies in his battles any more, and lets Thanatos loose. T4: sent down at last to Hades, Sisyphus has ONE last trick -- he tells his wife MEROPE not to bury him with the coin under his tongue for Charon. When he arrives, he complains to PERSEPHONE that his wife has neglected him and asks for one day back on earth to punish her -- and once released, refuses to return. He is only fetched back to the underworld by force by Hermes many years later, an old, old man. T5: his PUNISHMENT is famous -- he is set forever to roll a great BOULDER up a hill; every time he reaches the top, the boulder rolls back down, and he has to start again (Odyssey 11.593-600). Homer's Odysseus, visiting the underworld, sees him at his boulder: 'planting his feet, straining hard, with hands and feet he pressed the huge stone toward the crest; but just as he was about to heave it over the top, the boulder's weight would turn it back, and down again to the plain the shameless thing would roll.' Further rungs: Albert Camus made Sisyphus a modern philosophical figure in 'The Myth of Sisyphus' (1942) -- 'one must imagine Sisyphus happy'; the hill is not named in Homer; the exact reason for his punishment varies (some say for the tricking of Thanatos, some for the escape from Hades, some for both together).

Wrong tricks: Sisyphus tricks Death and Persephone (not Zeus or Hades directly).

name: Tantalus, Ixion, the Danaids: the underworld's punishment ward
scope: Three named eternal punishments in Tartarus. T1: three of the most famous mortals in Tartarus are TANTALUS, IXION, and the DANAIDS -- their fates are all forms of ETERNAL FUTILE ACTION, each fitted to the crime. T2: TANTALUS was king of LYDIA (or Phrygia) and a favourite guest at the gods' table -- until he stole AMBROSIA and NECTAR from Olympus to give to mortals, and (worse) served his own son PELOPS to the gods at a banquet to test whether they would notice. Demeter, distracted with grief for Persephone, ate a shoulder before the trick was found out; Pelops was restored to life by the gods with an IVORY SHOULDER-BLADE replacing the eaten one. T3: Tantalus's punishment is set in Tartarus -- he stands FOREVER in a POOL OF WATER UP TO HIS CHIN, with a fruit-laden BRANCH just above his head; whenever he stoops to drink, the water DRAINS AWAY, and whenever he reaches for the fruit, the branch LIFTS AWAY (Odyssey 11.582-592). The English verb 'tantalise' is his name. T4: IXION was king of the Lapiths in Thessaly -- he killed his own father-in-law by inviting him to a feast and pushing him into a pit of red-hot coals (the FIRST kin-murder in Greek myth); no mortal would purify him and Zeus generously took him in to Olympus as guest, but Ixion tried to seduce HERA. Zeus caught him -- and made a phantom Hera out of CLOUD (the cloud-woman NEPHELE), which Ixion embraced, and from that union came the CENTAURS (Pindar, Pythian 2.21-48). For attempted rape of a goddess Ixion was bound to a FIERY WHEEL, spinning forever through the sky (or through Tartarus, depending on the source). T5: the DANAIDS were the FIFTY DAUGHTERS of King DANAUS of Argos, forced to marry the fifty sons of their uncle Aegyptus; Danaus gave each daughter a dagger for the wedding night, and forty-nine of them murdered their bridegrooms in bed (only HYPERMNESTRA spared her husband Lynceus). For this the forty-nine are set in Tartarus forever to fill a great JAR with water -- and the jar has NO BOTTOM, or is FULL OF HOLES like a sieve, so no matter how many times they fetch water from the river, the jar is never full (Apollodorus 2.1.4). Further rungs: the fourth famous eternal-punishment case is Sisyphus (see own ladder); the fifth is TITYOS, a giant chained flat on his back while two VULTURES eat his liver (Odyssey 11.576-581 -- parallel to Prometheus's eagle, must be kept distinct); the term 'sisyphean' for a hopeless task, and 'tantalise' for teasing-out-of-reach, both come from this group.

Pelops's ivory shoulder: Pindar, Olympian 1.24-27. name: Arachne the weaver: challenging Athena
scope: The mortal spinner who out-wove a goddess, told in Ovid. T1: ARACHNE is a young mortal woman from HYPAEPA in Lydia (in Ovid; other versions say Colophon), daughter of a wool-dyer named Idmon; she is famous across all Asia Minor for her spinning and weaving, so extraordinary that the wood-nymphs of Lydia come down to watch her work. She boasts that she is BETTER THAN ATHENA HERSELF (Metamorphoses 6.5-25). T2: word reaches Athena, who comes down disguised as an OLD WOMAN and warns Arachne to be humbler, offering her a chance to withdraw the boast. Arachne insults the old woman and repeats the challenge -- 'let the goddess come and weave against me' -- at which Athena throws off her disguise and reveals herself in her divine form. The two set up looms and BEGIN A CONTEST (Metamorphoses 6.26-133). T3: ATHENA weaves a tapestry showing her OWN VICTORY over Poseidon for the naming of Athens, and around the borders FOUR CAUTIONARY SCENES of mortals punished for challenging the gods (Rhodope turned to a mountain, Antigone into a stork, etc.). Her weaving is flawless. T4: ARACHNE weaves a tapestry showing TWENTY-ONE SCENES of the GODS ABUSING MORTAL WOMEN -- Zeus as swan on Leda, Zeus as bull on Europa, Zeus as gold-shower on Danae, Poseidon as horse on Demeter, Poseidon as ram, Apollo as shepherd, all of them (Metamorphoses 6.103-128). Her weaving too is flawless -- so flawless that Athena cannot fault the workmanship. T5: enraged that a mortal has both matched her skill AND made her family look bad, Athena RIPS THE TAPESTRY DOWN and beats Arachne on the head with her boxwood shuttle. Arachne, in shame, hangs herself. Athena, pitying her (or in some versions still furious), sprinkles her with an herb and turns her into a SPIDER -- her body shrinks, her fingers become long thin legs, and she goes on spinning and weaving forever from a thread coming out of her own belly (Metamorphoses 6.134-145). The Greek word for spider is 'arachne', and every spider is her descendant. Further rungs: the tapestry-contest theme where a mortal makes divine subjects look bad is unusual in Greek myth -- Arachne's tapestry is a REAL critique embedded in the story (twenty-one scenes of gods being predatory); Ovid was writing under Augustus and had reasons to include such things obliquely; the scientific term for spiders, ARACHNIDS, is her name.

name: Marsyas, Midas, and the ass's ears
scope: Two music-contest stories that share a judge and a river. T1: ATHENA once invented the DOUBLE FLUTE (aulos), but seeing her cheeks puff up in the water's reflection while she played, she THREW IT AWAY in disgust -- and cursed anyone who picked it up. A SATYR named MARSYAS (from Phrygia in central Asia Minor) found it, learned to play it, and became so skilled that he grew proud and challenged APOLLO, the god of the LYRE, to a music contest -- flute against lyre. T2: the Muses (or in some versions the MUSES AND KING MIDAS of Phrygia) were made judges; the terms were set that the winner might do WHATEVER HE WISHED to the loser. Apollo played his lyre; Marsyas played his flute; the Muses judged Apollo the winner -- and in one version he won only after inverting his lyre and playing it upside-down and inviting Marsyas to do the same with the flute, which of course cannot be done. T3: Apollo's chosen punishment was HORRIFIC -- he had Marsyas hung upside-down from a PINE TREE and FLAYED ALIVE (Ovid, Metamorphoses 6.383-400). The satyr's blood and the tears of the woodland creatures who mourned him poured into the earth and became the RIVER MARSYAS in Phrygia (a real river, named for him even in classical times). Ovid's line: Marsyas cries out 'Why do you tear me from myself?' T4: in a PARALLEL contest, PAN the goat-god challenges Apollo, and this time KING MIDAS of Phrygia (the same king with the golden touch) is one of the judges (or the SOLE judge). Apollo plays; Pan plays; Midas alone judges for PAN over Apollo. T5: Apollo turns to Midas and says his ears must be as dull as an ANIMAL'S -- and turns Midas's ears into the ears of an ASS (Metamorphoses 11.146-193). Midas hides his ass's ears under a Phrygian cap; only his BARBER knows. Unable to keep the secret, the barber digs a hole in the ground and whispers into it 'King Midas has ass's ears', then covers the hole. A patch of REEDS grows there, and every time the wind blows the reeds whisper aloud 'King Midas has ass's ears' for the whole world to hear (Metamorphoses 11.180-193). Further rungs: Midas is more famous for his GOLDEN TOUCH -- given by Dionysus as thanks for the safe return of the drunken satyr Silenus, and quickly regretted when his own food and his daughter turn to gold; Midas washed the touch off in the river PACTOLUS, which is why the Pactolus in Lydia was famous for its gold-bearing sand (Metamorphoses 11.85-145); the double flute Athena threw away is called the aulos; the barber's Persian-cap comes from this story into art history.
source: PRIMARY: Ovid, Metamorphoses 6.383-400 (Marsyas flayed hanging from the pine, his blood becoming the river); Metamorphoses 11.85-193 (Midas's golden touch and washing it in the Pactolus, then the Pan-vs-Apollo contest with Midas as judge, ass's ears, the barber and the reeds); Herodotus 7.26 (mentions the river Marsyas at the sanctuary in Phrygia where Marsyas's skin was said to still be shown). name: Echo and Narcissus: the voice and the pool
scope: The nymph who could only repeat, and the boy who fell for his own reflection. T1: ECHO is an OREAD (mountain nymph) in the forests of Boeotia; she is punished by HERA for having distracted her with endless chatter while Zeus was off with the other nymphs -- Hera curses her so that she can no longer speak first, but can only REPEAT THE LAST WORDS anyone else has said (Ovid, Metamorphoses 3.359-369). T2: NARCISSUS is a beautiful young hunter, son of the river-god CEPHISSUS and the nymph Liriope; when he was born the seer TIRESIAS was asked if the child would live long, and answered 'YES -- IF HE NEVER KNOWS HIMSELF' (Metamorphoses 3.348) -- an oracle no one understood at the time. Every girl and boy who saw him falls in love, and he coldly rejects them all. T3: Echo sees him hunting in the forest and follows him from tree to tree, longing to speak but unable to begin. He calls out 'IS ANYONE HERE?' -- she calls back 'HERE!' 'COME!' -- 'COME!' 'LET US COME TOGETHER!' -- 'LET US COME TOGETHER!' She steps out to embrace him, and he shoves her away in disgust -- 'I would rather DIE than have you touch me' (Metamorphoses 3.379-392). Echo, humiliated, wastes away in the forest until only her VOICE remains, still repeating the last words spoken in lonely places. T4: a boy Narcissus once rejected prays to the goddess NEMESIS -- 'May he love as I have loved, and never win the loved one'. Nemesis hears; and one hot day, Narcissus stoops to drink from a clear POOL and sees a beautiful face rising toward him from the water. He does not realise it is his OWN REFLECTION -- he leans down to kiss it, but the water ripples; he reaches to embrace it, but the arms in the water reach up and dissolve at his touch (Metamorphoses 3.407-473). T5: he lies by the pool day and night, unable to eat, unable to leave, weeping at his own vanishing image; Echo watches from the trees and repeats his last words -- 'ALAS!' 'ALAS!' -- 'FAREWELL!' 'FAREWELL!' -- and he dies of longing for himself, and where his body lay the nymphs found only a flower with white petals and a golden centre, which we still call the NARCISSUS (Metamorphoses 3.501-510). Further rungs: Tiresias's oracle 'if he never knows himself' is understood only in retrospect -- Narcissus dies BECAUSE he finally knows himself in the water and cannot bear it; the English words 'echo' (a repeating voice) and 'narcissism' (self-love) are directly from these two.
source: PRIMARY: Ovid, Metamorphoses 3.339-510 (the whole story: Tiresias's prophecy at 348, Hera cursing Echo at 359-369, Echo's love and rejection at 379-401, Nemesis's answer at 405-406, the reflection at 407-473, the death at 474-510).
